2025_134_tcc_course_catalog_2025.paragraph: The 2024-2025 Course Description Book for Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS) sets out diploma requirements, course descriptions by department, online program offerings, Oakland Schools Technical Campus information, and the Troy School District nondiscrimination policy and antidiscrimination grievance procedure. Dr. Richard Machesky is identified as Superintendent of Schools and Mrs. Angela Milanov as principal of TCCHS at 1522 East Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083. The defining requirement is that TCCHS students must earn 19.5 credits for a Troy School District diploma, versus the 22.5 credits required for a Troy High School or Athens High School diploma.
2025_134_tcc_course_catalog_2025.page:
**Publication**
Course Description Book, 2024-2025, Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS), Troy School District. Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent of Schools. Mrs. Angela Milanov, Principal, 1522 East Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083, 248.823.5156. Department of Teaching & Learning, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, 248.823.5221.

**Nondiscrimination policy (revised August 2023)**
Cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, is appointed Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters; the District's Director of Special Education serves as Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Contact listed as John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

**Diploma and credit requirements**
TCCHS students must earn 19.5 credits; students seeking a Troy High School or Athens High School diploma must meet those schools' 22.5-credit requirement. TCCHS may allow students with demonstrated need to deviate from the 19.5-credit requirement through a meeting with a counselor or administrator. All TCCHS students must complete 8 semesters/4 years of high school and the 18 credits required by the Michigan Department of Education.

| Requirement (beginning with the Class of 2023) | Credits |
| --- | --- |
| English | 4.0 |
| Science (Biology 1.0, Chemistry 0.5, Physics 0.5, Science Elective 1.0) | 3.0 |
| Mathematics (Algebra 1 1.0, Geometry 1.0, Algebra 2 1.0, math elective/math-related in final year) | 4.0 |
| Social Studies (World History/Geography 1.0, American History/Geography 1.0, Economics 0.5, Government and Civics 0.5) | 3.0 |
| Personal Finance (embedded in Economics; required beginning with the class of 2028) | 0.5 |
| Physical Education/Health (PE 0.5, Health 0.5) | 1.0 |
| World Language | 2.0 |
| Visual, Performing, Applied Arts & Electives (VPAA 1.0, Elective 1.0) | 2.0 |
| TCCHS Program Requirements (Careers) | 0.5 |
| Online Learning Experience (20-hour, non-credit) | 0.0 |
| State Assessments | 0.0 |
| **Total** | **19.5** |

**Graduation requirement flexibility (updated 9.2015; MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b)**
Personal Curriculum; physical education credit through athletics, extracurricular activities, or counselor-approved PE class; World Language flexibility for heritage-language proficiency, international study and residence, or substitution of CTE or Visual & Performing or Applied Arts credits; and CTE program completion exchangeable on a 1:1 basis for science or world language credit, or to satisfy Algebra 2 through embedded content.

**Departments and courses**
Career Technical Education offers Woodworking Design & Fabrication 1, 2, and 3 (CAD, CNC, 3D printing). English offers Literature, Informational Reading and Writing, Communications, Creative Writing 1 and 2, Film and Literature, Literature of Suspense, Short Stories, Music Literature, Science Fiction, and Classical Mythology and Drama. Fine Arts offers Drawing 1, Advanced Drawing, Painting 1, Advanced Painting, Studio Art, Applied Arts and Design, Computer Graphics 1, Principles of Photography 1, and Intro to Music Technology and Recording. Mathematics offers Business Math in Algebra A/B, Geometry by Design, Personal Finance/Financial Well-Being, Algebra 1, Algebra 2, Geometry, Trigonometry, Financial Management, School-Based Enterprise, and Introduction to Probability and Statistics. Multi-Departmental offerings include Innovation Exploration, Innovation Learning, Innovation Lab, Careers, Design & Innovation Studio, Computer Science (Python), and Work Based Learning. Science offers Introductory Biology, Active Chemistry/Earth Science, Chemistry 1, Organic Chemistry, Introductory Physics, Physics 1, Forensic Science A/B, Environmental Science, and Human Impact on the Earth A/B. Social Studies offers Advanced Placement Art History, World History/Geography 1 and 2, American History/Geography 1 and 2, Economics, Government and Civics, and Conflicts of the 20th & 21st Centuries. World Language offers Spanish 1 through 4 and Spanish AP, delivered on the Edgenuity online platform.

**Online programs and OSTC**
The Inspire Online Program runs on Edgenuity and the Intersect Online Program on the Pearson Connexus platform, each with an extensive high school course list. Oakland Schools Technical Campus - Southeast (OSTC-SE) is at 5055 Delemere Street, Royal Oak, for grades 11-12, with a morning session (7:50 AM to 10:20 AM) and afternoon session (12:00 PM to 2:30 PM); the Northeast Campus in Pontiac offers Cosmetology. Applications are made online at www.ostconline.com by the end of February. OSTC credits are not NCAA approved.

**Grievance procedure**
A three-step formal antidiscrimination grievance process runs from the immediate supervisor or administrator to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services and finally to the Superintendent, whose decision is final and binding.
2025_134_tcc_course_catalog_2025.verbose:
Course Description Book for 2024-2025 at Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS), Troy School District, listing Dr. Richard Machesky as Superintendent of Schools and Mrs. Angela Milanov as principal. The school address is 1522 East Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083, telephone 248.823.5156. The Department of Teaching & Learning is listed at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, telephone 248.823.5221.

POLICY OF NONDISCRIMINATION (Revised August 2023). Addressed to students, parents, and citizens of the Troy School District, the policy statement cites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Troy School District states that it does not discriminate on the basis of sex or handicap in admission or access to, treatment or employment in, its programs and activities, and periodically reviews its educational and employment programs for compliance. A grievance procedure is available through any school office or through the Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator; bargaining-unit employees may alternatively use the grievance procedure in their collective bargaining agreement. In accordance with Federal regulations, the district has appointed Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, as Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters, and the District's Director of Special Education as Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions, suggestions, or concerns are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248)823-4000.

DIPLOMA AND CREDIT REQUIREMENTS. All students attending TCCHS must earn 19.5 credits to be eligible for a Troy School District high school diploma. Students interested in earning a diploma from Troy High School or Athens High School must meet the credit requirements in the THS and AHS course description book, totaling 22.5 credits. In alignment with the needs of alternative education students, TCCHS offers students with demonstrated need the opportunity to deviate from the 19.5-credit requirement; any TCCHS student may request a meeting with a counselor or administrator. All students enrolled at TCCHS must complete 8 semesters/4 years of high school and the 18 credits required by the Michigan Department of Education.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENT FLEXIBILITY OPTIONS (Updated 9.2015; MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b). Personal Curriculum allows students to earn additional credits in some core academic areas in lieu of requirements in other areas. Physical Education credit may be earned through athletics, extracurricular activities, or a counselor-approved PE class. The World Language requirement of 2.0 credits carries flexibility for non-English heritage language proficiency, international study and residence world language proficiency, and substitution of Career & Technical Education or Visual & Performing or Applied Arts credits. Students completing a Career & Technical Education program of study may exchange credits earned on a 1:1 basis for required credits in science or world language, or satisfy the Algebra 2 requirement by completing a CTE program with Algebra 2 content embedded.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS BEGINNING WITH THE CLASS OF 2023. English 4.0 credits, covering Literature, Informational Reading and Writing, Communications, and other English electives. Science 3.0 credits: Biology 1.0, Chemistry 0.5, Physics 0.5, Science Elective 1.0. Mathematics 4.0 credits: Algebra 1 1.0, Geometry 1.0, Algebra 2 1.0 (which may be met through CTE program completion, e.g., OSTC), plus a math elective or math-related course during the final year of high school. Social Studies 3.0 credits: World History/Geography 1.0, American History/Geography 1.0, Economics 0.5, Government and Civics 0.5. Personal Finance 0.5 credit, embedded into Economics and a graduation requirement for all students beginning with the class of 2028; students must take a TSD Economics or AP Economics course to be eligible. Physical Education/Health 1.0 credit (Physical Education 0.5, which may be earned through approved extracurricular athletics or activities, and Health 0.5). World Language 2.0 credits, satisfied by formal coursework or an equivalent K-12 learning experience, accepting 2.0 credits of world language (non-sequential accepted) or 1.0 credit of world language plus either 1.0 credit of CTE or 1.0 credit of Visual, Performing, or Applied Arts. Visual, Performing, Applied Arts & Electives 2.0 credits (1.0 VPAA, 1.0 elective). TCCHS Program Requirements 0.5 credit (Careers). Online Learning Experience 0.0 credits, a 20-hour non-credit online learning experience embedded in Troy classroom experiences throughout middle and high school. State Assessments 0.0 credits, requiring completion of State of Michigan required assessments as administered during high school. Total Credits 19.5.

CAREER TECHNICAL EDUCATION. Woodworking Design & Fabrication 1 (1/2 credit per semester, no prerequisite; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year) introduces designing, drawing, and manufacturing using CAD software, hand and power tools, power machines, and automation (CNC and 3D printing). Woodworking Design & Fabrication 2 (prerequisite Woodworking Design 1) emphasizes CAD and CNC design and production and advanced furniture and cabinet projects. Woodworking Design & Fabrication 3 (prerequisite Woodworking Design 2) continues the curriculum with heavy industry influence. Each carries 1/2 credit per semester and the same math-related credit provision.

ENGLISH DEPARTMENT. Literature (1/2 credit per semester, 4 semesters required, 2.0 credits total) uses a competency-based skill framework covering short stories, poetry, and novels, American literary eras, world literature, and forms of prose and verse. Informational Reading and Writing (1/2 credit per semester, 2 semesters required, 1.0 credit total) covers non-fiction and informational texts, data mining, note taking, synthesis, summarizing, and research. Communications (1/2 credit per semester, 1 semester required) covers non-verbal, verbal, visual, written, and communal styles, elements of journalism, debate, and public speaking. Creative Writing 1 (1 semester, 1/2 credit) is an elective for grades 10-12. Creative Writing 2 (prerequisite Creative Writing 1) covers poetry, essays, flash fiction, and short stories. Film and Literature covers film vocabulary, genre, film-making techniques, and film history. Literature of Suspense investigates authors including Edgar Allan Poe, Mary Shelley, and Stephen King. Short Stories emphasizes the American tradition. Music Literature examines music's role in culture and introduces Pro Tools recording software concepts. Science Fiction covers speculative literature. Classical Mythology and Drama explores myth and the origin of plays. Several English electives require successful completion of freshman year English.

FINE ARTS DEPARTMENT. Drawing 1; Advanced Drawing (prerequisite Drawing 1, with color as a focus); Painting 1 (water-soluble media); Advanced Painting (prerequisite Painting 1); Studio Art, with portfolio preparation as the goal and the option to be scheduled during Advanced Placement Art; Applied Arts and Design; Computer Graphics 1, teaching Photoshop along with art history and art theory; Principles of Photography 1, covering framing, composition, rule of thirds, light, texture, pattern lines, symmetry, depth of field, distance, perspective, culture, space, balance, color, and black and white photography; and Intro to Music Technology and Recording, using ProTools in a recording studio setting. Each is 1 semester, 1/2 credit.

HEALTH DEPARTMENT. Health (1 semester, 1/2 credit) covers healthy lifestyles, violence, sexual harassment, nutrition, fitness and weight control including steroids and eating disorders, alcohol and drug abuse, tobacco, human sexuality, birth control, and sexually transmitted diseases including HIV/AIDS. The course is required for graduation and is taken online through the Edgenuity platform.

MATHEMATICS DEPARTMENT. Business Math in Algebra A/B (Algebra 1 students)/Business Math A/B (Algebra 2 students), 4 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester, has students operate a business running an advanced fabrication lab customizing textile products and manufacturing items of wood, metal, and/or plastic, with proceeds self-funding the venture and supporting community service or monetary gifts to local charities; skills include sublimation, CNC operations, rapid prototyping, composite technologies, alternative energies, and automation robotics. Geometry by Design (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) integrates geometry with building and construction trades. Personal Finance/Financial Well-Being (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) is based on Michigan Personal Finance Competencies. Algebra 1 (2 semesters) covers linear, absolute value, quadratic, rational, polynomial, power, and exponential functions. Algebra 2 (prerequisite Algebra 1 and Geometry) covers the real number system, quadratics, sequences and series, polynomials, radicals, exponentials and logarithms, rational expressions, and introductory trigonometry and statistics. Geometry (prerequisite Algebra 1) covers triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, areas and volumes, trigonometry, similarity, congruence, and coordinate geometry. Trigonometry (1 semester, prerequisite Geometry and Algebra 2) covers radians and degrees, the unit circle, and trigonometric graphs. Financial Management (1 semester, 1/2 credit; satisfies 1/2 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year) includes a stock market game simulation and a budget challenge. School-Based Enterprise (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year) has students manage and operate a school store. Introduction to Probability and Statistics (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) covers probability, sampling, data distributions, linear and exponential relationships, and systems of linear equations.

MULTI-DEPARTMENTAL. Innovation Exploration (1 semester, 1/2 credit) covers job research, resume writing, interviewing, career portfolios, and mentor connections. Innovation Learning (1 semester, 1/2 credit) and Innovation Lab (prerequisite Innovation Learning) reference creatinginnovators.com and dschool.stanford.edu and are influenced by the D school at Stanford University, with the second semester devoted to a personal innovative project. Careers (1 semester, 1/2 credit) prepares students for the transition to post-secondary education and the workforce through cover letters, resumes, self-assessment profiles, and portfolios. Design & Innovation Studio (1 semester, 1/2 credit) uses design thinking and includes career and technical student organization (CTSO) activities and work-based learning (HQWBL) with local businesses. Computer Science (1 semester, 1/2 credit) teaches Python and earns 0.5 mathematics-related credit. Work Based Learning requires students to hold a job and work at least 8 hours weekly, with teacher worksite visits and supervisor goal-setting. Not all listed courses are offered each year.

PHYSICAL EDUCATION DEPARTMENT. 1 semester, 1/2 credit; Lifetime Fitness is taken online through the Edgenuity platform.

SCIENCE DEPARTMENT. Introductory Biology (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester). Active Chemistry/Earth Science (2 semesters) covers matter and atoms, chemistry of art, food chemistry, and chemistry of cleaning products. Chemistry 1 (2 semesters, prerequisite Algebra 1; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related graduation requirement during the 12th grade year). Organic Chemistry (1 semester, prerequisite Chemistry 1) includes melting point determination, distillation, and fermentation labs. Introductory Physics (2 semesters, prerequisite Introductory Biology and Algebra 1; satisfies 1 credit of the math-related requirement during the 12th grade year) fulfills the one-year chemistry-or-physics requirement under State of Michigan graduation requirements and aligns with the Michigan High School Content Standards and Expectations. Physics 1 (2 semesters) recommends completion of Geometry and enrollment in Algebra 2 and covers mechanics, waves, and electricity. Forensic Science A/B (2 semesters) covers crime scene procedures, evidence types, bone identification, entomology, pathology, fingerprinting, DNA, blood typing and blood spatter analysis, hair and fiber analysis, and handwriting analysis. Environmental Science (1 semester) includes field studies and water quality tests. Human Impact on the Earth A/B (2 semesters) covers weather, climate, geography, human cities, and climate change.

SOCIAL STUDIES DEPARTMENT. Advanced Placement Art History (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester). World History/Geography 1 (1 semester) runs from the collapse of Rome to the French Revolution and the defeat of Napoleon. World History/Geography 2 (1 semester) runs from the Industrial Revolution to current issues. American History/Geography 1 and 2 (2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester) cover the development of the United States from 1877. Economics (1 semester) covers economic systems, demand, supply, consumers and savers, trade, and the role of government. Government and Civics (1 semester) covers the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the federal system. Conflicts of the 20th & 21st Centuries (1 semester, 1/2 credit) examines total war, civil war, and limited war.

WORLD LANGUAGE DEPARTMENT. Spanish 1, 2, 3, and 4 and Spanish AP, each 2 semesters at 1/2 credit per semester with sequential prerequisites and teacher recommendation, all completed on the Edgenuity online platform. Spanish 1 targets Novice-mid to Novice-high proficiency on the ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines. Spanish AP follows College Board AP Spanish Language and Culture guidelines across the Interpretive, Interpersonal, and Presentational modes.

ONLINE PROGRAMS. The Inspire Online Program runs classes on the Edgenuity platform and the Intersect Online Program runs classes through the Pearson Connexus platform. The associated high school course list includes Advertising and Sales Promotion, African American Studies (Black History), Algebra 1 A/B, Algebra 2 variants, Algebra with Finance A/B, Animation 1 A/B, AP Biology A/B, AP Calculus AB A/B, AP English Language & Composition A/B, AP English Literature & Composition A/B, AP Environmental Science A/B, AP Human Geography A/B, AP Macroeconomics, AP Microeconomics, AP Psychology, AP Spanish A/B, AP Statistics A/B, AP U.S. Government and Politics, AP U.S. History A/B, Art History A/B, Art in World Cultures A/B, Astronomy A/B, Biology A/B, Business Applications, Calculus A/B, Chemistry A/B or Physics A/B, Coding 1 A/B, Consumer Math A/B, Digital Photography 1 A/B and 2, Earth Science A/B (Honors Available), Economics, English 9 through 12 A/B, Entrepreneurship A/B, Environmental Science A/B, Explorations in Math A/B, French 1-4 A/B, Fundamentals of English Composition, Game Design A/B, Game Design for Chromebooks A/B, Geography and Society, Geometry A/B, German 1-3 A/B, Gothic Literature, Government, Health, Health Fitness and Nutrition A/B, History of the Holocaust, Human Geography, International Business, Introduction to Drawing, Introduction to Grammar and Composition, Introduction to Graphic Design A/B, Living Music I & II, Marine Science A/B, Music Appreciation, Mythology and Folklore, Nutrition and Wellness, Personal Fitness, Personal Health and Safety with Sex Education, Physical Education and Physical Education II and III A/B, Physical Science A/B (Honors Available), Pre-Calculus A/B (Honors Available), Principles of Business & Finance A/B, Principles of Marketing A/B, Psychology A/B, Sociology 1 & 2, Spanish 1-4 A/B, Statistics A/B, U.S. History A/B, World Geography, and World History A/B.

OAKLAND SCHOOLS TECHNICAL CAMPUS. OSTC-SE is described as an extension of the home high school, with students attending their high school half the day and the technical campus the other half. Programs are organized into clusters staffed by instructors holding both a Michigan Teaching Certificate and Vocational Authorization. Several programs qualify students for advanced standing or college credit; students may attend for one or two years, with the second year providing advanced work, specialization, and a certificate of completion. Programs are offered to juniors and seniors on a selective basis, with OSTC recommending high school credit based on local district requirements, generally 1.5 credits per semester. If regular students carry six (6) credits, OSTC students must carry three (3) credits at their home high school in addition to three (3) credits at OSTC. Two sessions operate: Morning Session classes begin 7:50 AM and are dismissed 10:20 AM; Afternoon Session classes begin 12:00 PM and are dismissed 2:30 PM. Students apply online at www.ostconline.com by the end of February, with exploration tours for current sophomores and juniors in the fall. The Southeast Campus is at 5055 Delemere Street, Royal Oak, MI, north of 14 Mile between Crooks and Coolidge, serving grades 11-12, with course codes 08101 Session 1 AM and 08102 Session 2 PM. Southeast Campus programs listed are Automotive Technology (must begin in 11th grade), Collision Repair and Refinishing, Computer Programming, Computer Networking, Construction Technology, Culinary Arts/Hospitality, Electrical and Energy Technologies, Entrepreneurship & Advanced Marketing, Health Sciences, Machining, Mechatronics, Visual Imaging Technology, Welding, and Homeland Security (Criminal Justice or Cyber Security). The Northeast Campus in Pontiac, MI offers Cosmetology, which must begin in 11th grade. Credits offered at OSTC are not NCAA approved. A bus transports students to OSTC-SE and back; afternoon session students must provide their own transportation home from OSTC-SE or the high schools.

ANTIDISCRIMINATION GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE. Any student or employee who believes he or she has been discriminated against, denied a benefit, or excluded from participation based on sex (including sexual harassment), race, color, religion, national origin, age (employees only), height, weight, marital status, or handicap files a written grievance with the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, the designated compliance administrator; forms are available in the Employee Services Department. Step 1 requires a written grievance form to the immediate supervisor or administrator within 10 workdays of the incident; the administrator must send a copy to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services not later than the next workday; the supervisor or administrator meets with the grievant within 5 workdays of the filing date and gives a written answer within 3 workdays of the meeting. Step 2 requires appeal to the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services within 3 workdays of receipt of the answer; that official (or the Deputy Superintendent, if appropriate) meets with the grievant within 10 workdays of receipt of the appeal and gives a written answer within 5 workdays of the meeting. Step 3 requires appeal to the Superintendent within 3 workdays of receipt of the answer; the Superintendent meets with the grievant within 10 workdays of the appeal and gives a written answer within 5 workdays of the meeting, a decision that is final and binding on all parties. The Superintendent, Deputy Superintendent, and Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services may designate representatives. A grievance not filed or appealed within the specified time limits is conclusively deemed abandoned; failure of an administrator to hold a meeting or render a decision allows automatic appeal to the next level; time limits may be extended only by mutual written agreement. All records concerning a grievance are treated confidentially, and no record is kept in a staff member's personnel file if the final decision is that there was no reasonable basis for the grievance.

2025_135_nsk_12_troy_board_presentation_.paragraph: New Solutions K12 delivered a February 2025 board update to the Troy School District titled Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities and Other Students Who Struggle. The presentation lays out four project goals, the firm's credentials and those of Nate Levenson, a three-phase Phase 1 project plan, five commendations, five opportunity areas, and the district's current implementation efforts. The central recommendation set is to expand elementary reading specialists' reach, build general education teacher capacity, build coherent elementary schedules with time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention, implement best-practice extra-time intervention at the secondary level, and further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools.
2025_135_nsk_12_troy_board_presentation_.page:
**Presentation**
Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities & Other Students Who Struggle - Troy School District Board Update, February 2025, prepared by New Solutions K12 (www.newsolutionsk12.com).

**Project goals**
Develop an understanding of current practices related to special education and supporting all students who struggle; explore alignment of current practice with best practices; identify opportunities to raise student achievement and improve work-life balance for teachers and staff; craft a plan for implementing prioritized opportunities.

**About the firm and presenter**
New Solutions K12 describes serving over 300 districts in over 30 states, acting as lead partner for state departments of education in LA, CT, MD, VA, and VT, and staffing engagements with a former Superintendent, Special Ed Director, Principal, Instructional Coach, and teachers. Nate Levenson is described as a superintendent who closed the achievement gap in Arlington, MA, a consultant of over 15 years, and author of 6 books and 50+ whitepapers and articles. The firm states its best practices have been recommended by the U.S. Department of Education, cites a 66% reduction in achievement gap, and reports Louisiana results in which early adopters had the highest growth rates for students with disabilities on LEAP scores, all early adopters outpaced state average growth for students with disabilities by at least two-fold, some by three-fold and one by five-fold, nearly two thirds of high growth districts had top growth two years in a row, and one district's schools identified for low performance for students with disabilities dropped from 10 to 3.

**Phase 1 project plan**
Kickoff and engagement (assemble Guiding Coalition, share research on best practices, gather data on current practices); analysis (interviews and focus groups, analyze district data against benchmarks, develop key findings); share findings (highlight strengths and preliminary opportunities, discuss with the Guiding Coalition, prioritize and plan for implementation).

**Commendations**
Teachers are hardworking, dedicated, and caring; the district has the faith and confidence of parents and the community; the district has a deep understanding of reading best practices, particularly at the elementary level; the elementary Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) process is well defined and consistently implemented; the district has the desire and ability to serve students with severe needs in district.

**Opportunities**
1. Expand the reach of elementary reading specialists. 2. Build general education teacher capacity, including 2A ensuring students with mild to moderate disabilities work toward the same standards and curriculum, 2B expanding instructional coaching, and 2C improving integration of Special Education, ELD, and General Education by shifting responsibility to the general education teaching and learning team (with new teaching and learning and special education organizational charts). 3. Create comprehensive and coherent elementary schedules with sufficient time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention, using staggered intervention. 4. Implement best-practice secondary interventions, including 4A extra-time intervention from content strong teachers and 4B creating a sense of urgency for change. 5. Further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools.

**Best-practice intervention course criteria**
Extra time in addition to core; content strong teachers; graded/pass fail; credit bearing in high school; subject specific direct instruction targeted to specific skill gaps; approximately 15 students to a class; 40 plus minutes a day, five days a week; during the school day.

**Current implementation efforts**
Three key focus areas: re-organizing special education and general education leadership responsibilities (decision-making rights codified); defining and rolling out elementary 'non-negotiables' (two schools piloting); and expanding extra-learning time from content strong staff at the middle and high school levels, including sections/FTE needs, staffing and budgeting plans, and IEP change processes.

**Metrics**
Students with mild to moderate disabilities receive 100% of core instruction; equal access to extra-time intervention from content strong teachers; reading proficiency increases; secondary math and ELA proficiency increases. An appendix lists best-practice research and selected publications of Nate Levenson.
2025_135_nsk_12_troy_board_presentation_.verbose:
Board update presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education in February 2025 by New Solutions K12, titled Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities & Other Students Who Struggle.

PROJECT GOALS. Four goals are listed: (1) develop an understanding of current practices related to special education and supporting all students who struggle; (2) explore alignment of current practice with best practices; (3) identify opportunities to help raise achievement of students and improve work-life balance for teachers and staff; and (4) craft a plan for implementing prioritized opportunities.

ABOUT NEW SOLUTIONS K12. The firm describes an experienced team that has served over 300 districts in over 30 states; being trusted by state departments as lead partner for state departments of education in LA, CT, MD, VA, and VT; being bold yet practical, staffed by a former Superintendent, Special Ed Director, Principal, Instructional Coach, and teachers; and being evidence based, constantly conducting primary and secondary research. Nate Levenson is profiled as a superintendent who closed the achievement gap in Arlington, MA; a consultant of over 15 years and millions of miles; and an author of 6 books and 50+ whitepapers and articles. The presentation states that the firm's best practices have been recommended by the U.S. Department of Education and that the gains can be dramatic, citing a 66% reduction in achievement gap.

LOUISIANA RESULTS. The deck reports that early adopters had the highest growth rates for students with disabilities based on LEAP scores combining all grades and subjects; that all early adopters outpaced the state average growth for students with disabilities by at least two-fold (2X State Average); that some early adopters outpaced the state average by three-fold (3X State Average) and one early adopter by five-fold (5X State Average); that nearly two thirds of the high growth districts had top growth two years in a row; and that in one district the number of schools identified for low performance for students with disabilities dropped from 10 to 3.

PHASE 1 PROJECT PLAN. Three stages are described. Stage 1, Kickoff & Engagement: assemble a Guiding Coalition, share research on best practices, and gather data on current practices. Stage 2, Analysis: interviews and focus groups to build understanding, analyze district data and compare to benchmarks, and develop key findings. Stage 3, Share Findings: share findings that highlight strengths and preliminary areas of opportunity, discuss findings with the Guiding Coalition, and prioritize findings and plan for implementation.

SUMMARY OF COMMENDATIONS. Teachers are hardworking, dedicated, and caring. The district has the faith and confidence of its parents and the community. The district has a deep understanding of reading best practices, particularly at the elementary level. The elementary Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) process is well defined and consistently implemented. The district has the desire and ability to serve students with severe needs in district with its broad range of supports and services.

SUMMARY OF OPPORTUNITIES. (1) Expand the reach of elementary reading specialists to support more students who struggle. (2) Build general education teacher capacity to take greater responsibility for all students' success, with sub-items 2A ensure students with mild to moderate disabilities are working toward the same standards and utilize the same curriculum; 2B expand instructional coaching to reach a greater number of teachers; and 2C improve integration of Special Education, ELD, and General Education by shifting responsibility for programming and support for nearly all students to the general education teaching and learning team. (3) Create comprehensive and coherent schedules at the elementary level to define and include sufficient time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention. (4) Implement best-practice interventions at the secondary level for nearly all students, with 4A embrace extra time intervention from content strong teachers for students with disabilities and 4B create a sense of urgency for change. (5) Further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools in the district to accelerate implementation of recommended best practices.

OPPORTUNITY 1 DETAIL. The deck states that students with disabilities are not yet achieving at high levels, that this is common even in high performing districts, and that the district is proactively addressing the challenges. It urges that students with disabilities not be excluded from best practice interventions. An illustration shows that across four classrooms, five students are struggling with phonics, and argues that interventionists should group all five students with common needs, since grouping by area of need makes intervention easier for staff and more impactful for students.

OPPORTUNITY 2 DETAIL. Under 2b, expanding instructional coaching, the deck lists elements of good teaching: begin a lesson with a short review of previous learning; present new material in small steps with student practice after each step; ask many questions and incorporate multiple opportunities for student response; think aloud and provide models; guide students as they begin to practice; check for understanding and provide systematic feedback and corrections; provide scaffolds for difficult tasks; have students express their ideas verbally as scaffolding for writing; provide ongoing opportunities for review and practice; and teach skills and strategies that increase self-determination so students achieve their goals with greater independence, under the heading Good Teaching Is Good Teaching. Under 2C, the deck presents a new Teaching and Learning organizational chart and a new Special Education organizational chart.

OPPORTUNITY 3 DETAIL. Creating comprehensive and coherent elementary schedules is illustrated with the point that staggering intervention expands the reach of teachers.

OPPORTUNITY 4 DETAIL. Implementing best-practice interventions at the secondary level for all students who struggle academically is framed as Core Instruction plus Extra Time to Learn equaling Mastery, with the observation that most of the widely used current supports do not provide students with extra-time intervention from content strong staff. Best practice intervention courses are defined as including extra time in addition to core; content strong teachers; graded/pass fail; credit bearing in high school; subject specific, direct instruction targeted to specific skill gaps; approximately 15 students to a class; 40 plus minutes a day, five days a week; and during the school day.

OPPORTUNITY 5 DETAIL. District wide expectations might be established for who receives intervention; who provides intervention instruction; how intervention fits into the master schedule; when special education intervention should differ from general education intervention; expectations for work load, use of time, group size, and total students served for literacy specialists and other interventionists; and expectations for workload, use of time, and total teachers supported for instructional coaches.

CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION EFFORTS. Three identified key focus areas are: (1) defining and re-organizing the responsibilities of the special education and general education leadership teams, for which clear decision-making rights have been codified; (2) clearly defining and rolling out non-negotiables at the elementary level; and (3) expanding extra-learning time from content strong staff at the middle and high school levels. The elementary non-negotiables defined and agreed to are: all students receive 100% of core reading and math; interventions and supports are taught by teachers with content expertise; intervention is grouped by student area of need; interventions are aligned to high quality tier 1 core curriculum; students with mild to moderate disabilities have full access to best practice interventions; and IEPs will be updated to reflect best practice interventions. Two schools are piloting, and continued support is underway to detail a roll-out plan. For the secondary work, continued support is underway to finalize what extra-time intervention at the secondary level will look like; identify how many sections and FTE will be needed for intervention at each school; create a staffing and budgeting plan to adequately staff intervention; create a plan to ensure all students who need it, including students with mild to moderate disabilities, access these intervention classes next year; document a process for changing IEPs as needed; and support building strategic schedules that support extra-time intervention.

END STATE AND METRICS. The stated end state is that all elementary students will receive reading best practice core and intervention; all secondary students will receive best practice intervention including extra time from content strong staff; and the district will have a means to monitor both implementation and outcomes. The metrics identified as mattering most are: students with mild to moderate disabilities receive 100% of core instruction; students with disabilities have equal access to extra time intervention from content strong teachers; reading proficiency scores increase for students with and without disabilities; and math and ELA proficiency scores at the secondary level increase for students with and without disabilities.
